1: The one who does the action that ought to be done, without depending on the fruit of action, is both a renouncer and a yogī. It is not the one who keeps no fire, nor the one who performs no rites.
2: What they call renunciation, son of Pāṇḍu, know that to be yoga. For no one becomes a yogī without having renounced intention.
3: For the sage who wishes to climb to yoga, action is said to be the means. Once that same sage has climbed to yoga, stillness is said to be the means.
4: For when one clings neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions, and has renounced all intentions, then one is said to have climbed to yoga.
5: One should lift up the self by the self, and should not let the self sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
6: The self is a friend to the person who has mastered the self by the self. But for one who has not mastered the self, the self itself would act with hostility, like an enemy.
7: In one who has mastered the self and is at peace, the highest self stays collected in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and likewise in honour and dishonour.
8: The yogī whose self is content with knowledge and discernment, who stands at the peak with senses conquered, and to whom a clod of earth, a stone and gold are the same, is called yoked.
9: One whose buddhi is the same toward well-wishers, friends and foes, toward the indifferent, those who stand in the middle, the hateful and kinsmen, and even toward the good and the wicked, stands out.
10: The yogī should constantly yoke the self, staying in a secluded place, alone, with thought and self restrained, free of wishes and without possessions.
11: In a clean place one should set up a firm seat for oneself, neither too high nor too low, with cloth, a hide and kuśa grass laid on top.
12: There, sitting down on that seat, with the mind made one-pointed and the activity of thought and senses restrained, one should practise yoga to purify the self.
13: One should hold body, head and neck even and unmoving, stay steady, and gaze at the tip of one's own nose without looking off in any direction.
14: With the self made calm and fear gone, established in the vow of a celibate student, with the mind restrained and set on me, one should sit yoked, holding me as the highest.
15: Always yoking the self in this way, the yogī whose mind is controlled reaches the peace that abides in me, the peace whose highest point is nirvāṇa.
16: But yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all. It is not for one given to too much sleep, Arjuna, nor indeed for one who stays awake.
17: For one who is measured in food and recreation, measured in effort in actions, and measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.
18: When the well-controlled mind rests in the self alone, and one is free of longing for all desires, then one is called yoked.
19: A lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker: that is the comparison remembered for the yogī whose mind is restrained, practising the yoga of the self.
20: There is a state where the mind, held in check by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and where indeed one sees the self by the self and is content in the self.
21: There one knows that endless happiness which buddhi can grasp and which lies beyond the senses, and once established there, one does not move from the truth.
22: Having gained it, one thinks no other gain greater than that, and established in it, one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow.
23: One should know that state, the undoing of the union with sorrow, as what is named yoga. That yoga is to be practised with resolve and with a mind that does not despair.
24: One should give up all the desires born of intention, leaving none, and with the mind alone bring the whole group of the senses under control on every side.
25: Then little by little one should come to rest, by means of buddhi held steady with firmness. Having made the mind abide in the self, one should not think of anything at all.
26: Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, one should restrain it from there and bring it under control in the self alone.
27: For the highest happiness comes to this yogī, whose mind is calm, whose rajas is stilled, who has become brahman and is without stain.
28: Always yoking the self in this way, the yogī, with stain gone, easily attains the touch of brahman, which is endless happiness.
29: One whose self is yoked by yoga, and who sees the same everywhere, sees the self abiding in all beings and all beings in the self.
30: To one who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me, I am not lost, and that one is not lost to me.
31: The yogī who rests on oneness and worships me as abiding in all beings lives in me, in whatever way that yogī may be living.
32: The yogī who, by comparison with oneself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether it is happiness or sorrow, is thought the highest.
33: This yoga that you have declared to be sameness, slayer of Madhu: I do not see any steady footing for it, because of restlessness.
34: The mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa: turbulent, strong and stubborn. Holding it back seems to me as hard as holding back the wind.
35: No doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But with practice, son of Kuntī, and with dispassion, it can be held.
36: Yoga is hard to reach for one whose self is unrestrained: that is my view. But one who strives, with the self under control, can reach it through the right means.
37: One who has faith but does not strive, whose mind has strayed from yoga and who has not reached full success in yoga: what course does that person take, Kṛṣṇa?
38: Fallen from both, does that person not perish like a torn cloud, mighty-armed one, without footing and bewildered on the path of brahman?
39: You ought to cut away this doubt of mine, Kṛṣṇa, leaving nothing of it. For no one other than you can be found to cut this doubt.
40: Son of Pṛthā, neither here nor in the next world is there destruction for that person. For no one who does good, dear one, ever takes a bad course.
41: One who has fallen from yoga reaches the worlds of those who have done deeds of merit, dwells there for unending years, and is then born in the house of the pure and prosperous.
42: Or else that person is born right into a family of wise yogīs. For a birth such as this is harder to obtain in the world.
43: There that person gains the union with buddhi that belonged to the former body, and from there strives again toward full success, joy of the Kurus.
44: For that same former practice carries such a person along, even without their willing it. Even one who wishes to know about yoga goes beyond the brahman of words.
45: But the yogī who strives with effort, whose faults are fully cleansed, and who has been made perfect through many births, then goes on to the highest course.
46: The yogī is greater than the ascetics, is held to be greater even than those who know, and is greater than those who do actions. Therefore become a yogī, Arjuna.
47: Even among all yogīs, the one who is full of faith and worships me with the inner self gone to me is the one I hold to be most fully joined in yoga.
